Version: 1 Date: 21 Dec 2020
Author’s response to reviews:
21st December 2020
Dear Dr Lin Lee,
Re: Response to peer review comments on the manuscript‘Characteristics and mortality rates
among patients requiring intermediate care: a national cohort study using linked databases’
Thank you for considering the above manuscript for publication. We have reviewed the peer
review comments received and amended the manuscript accordingly. We thank the peer reviewers
for their consideration of the manuscript and helpful comments. We consider our response has
enhanced the quality, clarity and potential impact of the findings. Overall, the study was viewed as
important for clinical care and policy by conducting robust analysis of national data to address a
relatively neglected area of care for older people. The table below details each reviewers’
comments and our response. All changes made are highlighted in the revised manuscript.
Thank you in anticipation for your consideration of this revised manuscript.
On behalf of the co-authors
Yours sincerely,
Catherine J Evans

Peer review comments and the author response:
Reviewer 1
Thank you for sending me this manuscript to review. It was a pleasure to read. It is extremely well
written and concise in it's reporting. I commend the authors for completing such important work
and adhering to a rigorous methodology. I have only very minor comments for the authors, which I
leave to their discretion as to whether or not any changes are made. As I said, these are extremely
minor points as overall, I thought the paper was extremely interesting and of a very high standard
Thank you for your comments detailing the importance and strength of the manuscript.
On lines 171 - 172, it would be helpful to have the percentages to the n values of total numbers
from cancer and non-cancer. I find it really interesting that only 5% of the total sample were
cancer. I am surprised that this isn't addressed more in the results/discussion - particularly in the
light of cancer having the most predictable disease trajectory.
We have included in the results the respective proportional size for the cancer and non-cancer
groups. We have detailed in the limitations the small proportion of the cancer group (4.8%) in the
cohort, potential under-reporting with inclusion limited to cancer as the main diagnosis on the
index, as opposed to a history of cancer (lines 319-321).
Figure 1 appears to be missing some text - in the second box "368......". I assume this is cancer
admissions? If I was being pedantic, I would expect the exclusion arrows on the figure to point the
other way (towards the exclusion boxes).
Thank you, we have corrected this typo. We agree the exclusion arrows are clearer pointing to
the exclusion boxes. We have amended to show this.
I see a reference to SPACE on the authorship list, but no further information is given on this
group.Thank you for noting this omission.
We have detailed in the acknowledgement that the manuscript is part of a larger study, stating in
full the study acronym SPACE, and the Steering groups members (line 374-376).
Reviewer 3
The paper aims to investigate the factors associated with death within 1 year of admission to an
intermediate care unit, in order to inform priorities for high-quality care for older people. The
paper is novel and adds value and uses a large sample investigating several factors. However, the
paper is hard to read and would benefit from more clarity and more succinct writing throughout.
Thank you for your comments detailing the importance and strength of the manuscript. We have
reviewed and amended the manuscript to improve the clarity in the writing.
The title does not seem to clearly reflect the aim of the paper. 'Characteristics and mortality rates of
patients requiring intermediate care: a national cohort study using linked databases'

Thank you this is a helpful suggestion for the title that reflects more accurately the aim of the
manuscript and reporting. We have amended the title accordingly.
Abstract:
Background: The first two sentences do not flow very well and would benefit from rewriting. Is it
necessary to use the term 'nearness to end of life' or would just 'end of life' be sufficient?
We have reworded to improve clarity and flow.
Results: Would the word 'individual' be more appropriate than 'unique'
We have just stated adults. We stated unique to convey that each adult was only counted once in
the cohort, but this seems implicit.
Conclusion: Should include a greater focus on the integration of palliative care as is presented in
the conclusion of the manuscript
Thank you, we have included in the abstract conclusion main message of requirement of greater
integration of palliative care.
Background:
Paragraph one would benefit from rewriting in order to improve the flow of text and clarity for the
reader
Thank you, we have revised this opening background paragraph to improve clarity and flow.
The sentence 'Inherent is an uncertain illness trajectory over many years' could be written more
clearly
We have revised to improve clarity (line 55-56)
Line 78: It is generally advised to avoid using the term 'we' in manuscripts. It should be made clear
within the text that this review is unpublished
We have re-worded this sentence to indicate that the study was preceded by a systematic review
and referring the reader to the additional file and stating that unpublished (lines 76-77).
Lines 81-83: Sentence is long, could be reworded to improve clarity
Thank you, we have revised to improve clarity.
Methods:
The term 'we' is used throughout and should be removed.
We have minimised the use of reporting in the first person, in line with BMC Medicine editorial
style.
Line 94: "we used the term intermediate care unit in the publication" not necessary as you have
defined what it means
Thank you, we have deleted this sentence.
Line 120: It would be useful to clarify what is meant by the term 'index admission' as this may not
be something all readers are familiar with

We have defined index admission as the first admission in the 12-month reporting period (lines
104-106).
Line 138-139: more detail is needed here as it is unclear what covariates were used.
Thank you, we have clarified in the methods that all variables detailed in table 1 describing the
cohort were considered in the survival model.
Line 143: More detail is needed to specify what kind of stepwise regression was used and the
reason why the particular method was chosen.
A more detailed analysis plan and justification is presented in Additional File B. We have included
this as additional information for readers seeking to understand fully the type of stepwise
regression and rationale.
No mention that non-cancer included those with co-morbid diagnosis of cancer till limitations. Is
there any way this could be incorporated into the analysis as it doesn't seem to be an accurate
reflection of the data if some of the non-cancer group do in fact have cancer.
Thank you it is important to include this in the methods for clarity. We have stated in the
methods that individuals with a main diagnosis of a non-cancer condition may have had a history
of cancer, but this was not the main reported reason for the admission (line 146-147). To avoid
repetition, we have not re-stated this point in the limitations.
Results:
Line 163: as mentioned in the abstract, 'individual' rather than 'unique'
Thank you, we have revised to state individual.
Line 170: very low levels of non-white population are included in the sample, lower than the non-
white representation in the population. Perhaps some discussion of this should be included,
perhaps more people from non-white populations are cared for at home.
The cohort included all adults admitted to an eligible intermediate care unit in 2016. The lower
than national average of non-white representation likely reflects the location of these facilities in
mainly urban/rural settings (not cities that are generally ethnically more diverse) and the older age
of the population which has higher proportion of White ethnicity than the national population.
Line 174-181: not sure all this information is needed as it is presented in the table, this section
could be significantly reduced and the reader referred to the table.
Thank you, we have reduced the information to report only the main points.
Is the figure labelling correct? Figure 2b is listed as age but line 190-192 talks about diseases when
referring to figure 2b
Thank you for spotting this. We have updated Figure 2b to show main diagnosis and survival.
Line 209: please explain what model's concordance means to make it easier for readers unfamiliar
with these statistical tests to understand

We have defined in the methods“The models were selected that had the maximum concordance
statistics (a measure of goodness of fit)…. (line 152). In the results, stated "The model showed a
good fit with high concordance at 0·725."
Line 212: refers to post-acute admission but the table says hospital, keep consistent throughout,
maybe use hospital in brackets
Thank you, we have amended to state hospital to maintain consistency in the reporting.
Discussion:
Line 234-236 long sentence, requires rewording to improve clarity
Thank you we have re-worded.
Line 240-242 as above, unclear what the authors mean here
Thank you we have re-worded.
The authors state that better integration is needed with palliative care. Do we know from this data
if patients had access to palliative care, it may be that some patients had received referrals but
received outpatient palliative care assistance. The paper would benefit from some discussion of
this point.
Thank you this is an important point. We have stated in the discussion that provision of palliative
care is a commonly cited function of intermediate care units, but provision varies widely with little
information about the contribution of palliative care advice and support (line 269-271).
Unfortunately, reporting on the receipt of palliative care in the HSE data is very limited and too
weak to describe the provision in a meaningful way.
Line 260-263 not sure that the reference to covid is relevant here, if it is included it needs to be
linked better as at present it doesn't seem to fit
Thank you, we have amended to keep to the point of high risk of poor outcome of death for older
people with multimorbidity and chronic conditions, with COIVD-19 cited as a profound example
of this.
310-311 seems a major flaw to include those with cancer diagnosis in the non-cancer group
We have made explicit throughout the manuscript that the overarching groups of cancer or non-
cancer conditions were identified from the main diagnosis on the index admission (the first
admission).
Reviewer 4
Thank you for the opportunity to review this article, the paper reports on a well conducted analysis
in a relatively neglected setting. End of life care for older adults is an important area, and a
strength of this study is its comprehensiveness in sample size and representation of the patient
population. The addition of the systematic review and contextualisation within the findings adds to
the strength of the research, and the methods and results section are refreshingly thorough.
Thank you for your supportive comments on the importance and the robustness of this work.
Main points:

Abstract - The methods/results sections of the main paper are easy to follow and understandable,
however at times the corresponding sections in the abstract are difficult to follow. Consider
simplifying the abstract.
Thank you, we have reviewed the abstract and improved the clarity and flow in the background
and conclusions.
It is unclear at times whether the research is located in end of life care for those with chronic
conditions, or specifically for older adults. A sentence stating that the setting is open to adults,
however is predominantly utilised by older adults, would clarify this.
Thank you for this important point. We have clarified that these settings care typically for adults
with chronic progressive conditions and increasingly a mainly older population (lines 62-63).
At times, the introduction and discussion feel slightly abstract in reference to the experience of
patients within these settings. If there is qualitative research available in this area, the paper would
benefit from some discussion of how patients are admitted to such settings, i.e. what differentiates
between those who are discharged to care homes, and the care received.
Thank you this is an important comment about experiences of patients and family carers using
these facilities. We have cited qualitative work reporting on this in the introduction (lines 69-72),
and in the discussion (lines 271-272)
The discussion is repetitive of the results at times (pages 11 and 12), this could be shortened and
instead a wider discussion regarding the position and importance of intermediate care units within
the wider long term care system for older adults, and subsequent need for end of life care
provision, could be added.
Thank you we agree. We have removed repetition of reporting on the results in the discussion. We
have instead given more detailed consideration on the importance of intermediate care units within
the continuum of services for older people, and how our findings inform priorities for care in these
settings (lines 263-269).
Minor points:
Abstract - it is unclear if the study is limited to older adults, or that the setting is disproportionality
used by older adults. It would be useful to clarify this early on.
Thank you, we have clarified this stating in the abstract that these facilities support mainly older
adults.
Abstract - change 2016 dates to "over a one year period in 2016".
Thank you this is simpler. We have incorporated this suggestion.
Abstract - "We explored the cohort by non-cancer and cancer with significant differences in
mortality" - reword this sentence
We have revised this sentence to improve clarity.
Abstract - "At 0-28 days post-admission, risks were highest (reference: Musculoskeletal disorders)
for respiratory conditions (pneumonia aHR 6·17 [95% CI 4·90-7·76], chronic obstructive
pulmonary disease (aHR 5·01 [95% CI 3·78-6·62]), dementia (aHR 5·07 [95% CI 3·80- 6·77]),
liver disease (aHR 9·75 [95% CI 6·50-14·6]) and (reference cancer 'other') lung cancer (aHR 1·20
[95% CI 1·04-1·39])." - this isn't clear, it may be worth rewording as "At 0-28 days post-

admission, risks were highest for XX, XX and XX, when compared to (reference). Report non
cancer and cancer in separate sentences.
Thank you, we have revised following your suggestions to improve clarity.
Abstract - "Highest multi-morbidity (reference: lowest) at 0-28 days showed for non-cancer aHR
2·57 [95% CI 2·36-2·79] and cancer aHR 2·59 [95% CI 2·13-3·15]." - reword this sentence.
Thank you, we have revised following your suggestions to improve clarity.
Consider changing the aHR to HR and clarify in the text that they are adjusted - the use of HR
would not imply that the hazard ratio is not adjusted and aHR is uncommon in usage (in my
experience).
Thank you, we have reviewed the reporting style in BMC Medicine. Statistical reporting typically
states adjusted HR when used. We have kept the reporting in this manner and can amend if
advised by the editor.
Page 7 line 144: "using bidirectional selection with an entry criterion 145 of 0·1 and retention
criterion of 0·05" - clarify that these refer to p values.
Thank you we have stated“…p value entry criterion..”(line 147)
Table 2 - highlight significant findings in bold or star them.
We have put in bold significant findings in table 2 and table 3 reporting the factors associated with
mortality for the two groups.
Figure 1 - second box down needs "cancer admissions" adding.
Thank you, we have corrected this typo.
Kaplan Meier curves - in my view, the numbers at risk are not required as the figures illustrate the
point well enough.
We agree that the information is detailed in the figure, but we have retained the numbers at risk as
this is advocated in the STROBE reporting guidance.
The term "unique" is used too often, consider rewording.

Reviewer's report:
Thank you for sending me this manuscript to review. It was a pleasure to read. It is extremely well
written and concise in it's reporting. I commend the authors for completing such important work
and adhering to a rigorous methodology. I have only very minor comments for the authors, which I
leave to their discretion as to whether or not any changes are made.
1. On lines 171 - 172, it would be helpful to have the percentages to the n values of total numbers
from cancer and non-cancer. I find it really interesting that only 5% of the total sample were
cancer. I am surprised that this isn't addressed more in the results/discussion - particularly in the
light of cancer having the most predictable disease trajectory.
2. Figure 1 appears to be missing some text - in the second box "368......". I assume this is cancer
admissions? If I was being pedantic, I would expect the exclusion arrows on the figure to point the
other way (towards the exclusion boxes).
3. I see a reference to SPACE on the authorship list, but no further information is given on this
group.
As I said, these are extremely minor points as overall, I thought the paper was extremely
interesting and of a very high standard.
Thank you.

Reviewer’s report
Title: Characteristics and mortality rates among patients requiring intermediate care: a national
cohort study using linked databases
Version: 0 Date: 29 Nov 2020
Reviewer's report:
Thank you for the opportunity to review this article, the paper reports on a well conducted analysis
in a relatively neglected setting. End of life care for older adults is an important area, and a
strength of this study is its comprehensiveness in sample size and representation of the patient
population. The addition of the systematic review and contextualisation within the findings adds to
the strength of the research, and the methods and results section are refreshingly thorough.
Main points:
*Abstract - The methods/results sections of the main paper are easy to follow and understandable,
however at times the corresponding sections in the abstract are difficult to follow. Consider
simplifying the abstract.
*It is unclear at times whether the research is located in end of life care for those with chronic
conditions, or specifically for older adults. A sentence stating that the setting is open to adults,
however is predominantly utilised by older adults, would clarify this.
*At times, the introduction and discussion feel slightly abstract in reference to the experience of
patients within these settings. If there is qualitative research available in this area, the paper would
benefit from some discussion of how patients are admitted to such settings, i.e. what differentiates
between those who are discharged to care homes, and the care received.
*The discussion is repetitive of the results at times (pages 11 and 12), this could be shortened and
instead a wider discussion regarding the position and importance of intermediate care units within
the wider long term care system for older adults, and subsequent need for end of life care
provision, could be added.
Minor points:
*Abstract - it is unclear if the study is limited to older adults, or that the setting is
disproportionality used by older adults. It would be useful to clarify this early on.
*Abstract - change 2016 dates to "over a one year period in 2016".
*Abstract - "We explored the cohort by non-cancer and cancer with significant differences in
mortality" - reword this sentence.
*Abstract - "At 0-28 days post-admission, risks were highest (reference: Musculoskeletal
disorders) for respiratory conditions (pneumonia aHR 6·17 [95% CI 4·90-7·76], chronic
obstructive pulmonary disease (aHR 5·01 [95% CI 3·78-6·62]), dementia (aHR 5·07 [95% CI
3·80- 6·77]), liver disease (aHR 9·75 [95% CI 6·50-14·6]) and (reference cancer 'other') lung
cancer (aHR 1·20 [95% CI 1·04-1·39])." - this isn't clear, it may be worth rewording as "At 0-28
days post-admission, risks were highest for XX, XX and XX, when compared to (reference).
Report non cancer and cancer in separate sentences.
*Abstract - "Highest multi-morbidity (reference: lowest) at 0-28 days showed for non-cancer aHR
2·57 [95% CI 2·36-2·79] and cancer aHR 2·59 [95% CI 2·13-3·15]." - reword this sentence.

*Consider changing the aHR to HR and clarify in the text that they are adjusted - the use of HR
would not imply that the hazard ratio is not adjusted and aHR is uncommon in usage (in my
experience).
*Page 7 line 144: "using bidirectional selection with an entry criterion 145 of 0·1 and retention
criterion of 0·05" - clarify that these refer to p values.
*Table 2 - highlight significant findings in bold or star them.
*Figure 1 - second box down needs "cancer admissions" adding.
*Kaplan Meier curves - in my view, the numbers at risk are not required as the figures illustrate the
point well enough.
*The term "unique" is used too often, consider rewording.

The paper aims to investigate the factors associated with death within 1 year of admission to an
intermediate care unit, in order to inform priorities for high-quality care for older people. The
paper is novel and adds value and uses a large sample investigating several factors. However, the
paper is hard to read and would benefit from more clarity and more succinct writing throughout.
The title does not seem to clearly reflect the aim of the paper. 'Characteristics and mortality rates of
patients requiring intermediate care: a national cohort study using linked databases'
Abstract:
Background: The first two sentences do not flow very well and would benefit from rewriting. Is it
necessary to use the term 'nearness to end of life' or would just 'end of life' be sufficient?
Results: Would the word 'individual' be more appropriate than 'unique'
Conclusion: Should include a greater focus on the integration of palliative care as is presented in
the conclusion of the manuscript
Background:
Paragraph one would benefit from rewriting in order to improve the flow of text and clarity for the
reader. The sentence 'Inherent is an uncertain illness trajectory over many years' could be written
more clearly
Line 78: It is generally advised to avoid using the term 'we' in manuscripts. It should be made clear
within the text that this review is unpublished
Lines 81-83: Sentence is long, could be reworded to improve clarity
Methods
The term 'we' is used throughout and should be removed.
Line 94: "we used the term intermediate care unit in the publication" not necessary as you have
defined what it means
Line 120: It would be useful to clarify what is meant by the term 'index admission' as this may not
be something all readers are familiar with
Line 138-139: more detail is needed here as it is unclear what covariates were used.
Line 143: More detail is needed to specify what kind of stepwise regression was used and the
reason why the particular method was chosen.
No mention that non-cancer included those with co-morbid diagnosis of cancer till limitations. Is
there any way this could be incorporated into the analysis as it doesn't seem to be an accurate
reflection of the data if some of the non-cancer group do in fact have cancer.
Results
Line 163: as mentioned in the abstract, 'individual' rather than 'unique'

Line 170: very low levels of non-white population are included in the sample, lower than the non-
white representation in the population. Perhaps some discussion of this should be included,
perhaps more people from non-white populations are cared for at home.
Line 174-181: not sure all this information is needed as it is presented in the table, this section
could be significantly reduced and the reader referred to the table.
Is the figure labelling correct? Figure 2b is listed as age but line 190-192 talks about diseases when
referring to figure 2b
Line 209: please explain what model's concordance means to make it easier for readers unfamiliar

Line 212: refers to post-acute admission but the table says hospital, keep consistent throughout,

Reviewer's report:
Thank you for sending me this manuscript to review. It was a pleasure to read. It is extremely well
written and concise in it's reporting. I commend the authors for completing such important work
and adhering to a rigorous methodology. I have only very minor comments for the authors, which I
leave to their discretion as to whether or not any changes are made.
1. On lines 171 - 172, it would be helpful to have the percentages to the n values of total numbers
from cancer and non-cancer. I find it really interesting that only 5% of the total sample were
cancer. I am surprised that this isn't addressed more in the results/discussion - particularly in the
light of cancer having the most predictable disease trajectory.
2. Figure 1 appears to be missing some text - in the second box "368......". I assume this is cancer
admissions? If I was being pedantic, I would expect the exclusion arrows on the figure to point the
other way (towards the exclusion boxes).
3. I see a reference to SPACE on the authorship list, but no further information is given on this
group.
As I said, these are extremely minor points as overall, I thought the paper was extremely
interesting and of a very high standard.
Thank you.

Title: Characteristics and mortality rates among patients requiring intermediate care: a national
cohort study using linked databases
Version: 0 Date: 29 Nov 2020
Reviewer's report:
Thank you for the opportunity to review this article, the paper reports on a well conducted analysis
in a relatively neglected setting. End of life care for older adults is an important area, and a
strength of this study is its comprehensiveness in sample size and representation of the patient
population. The addition of the systematic review and contextualisation within the findings adds to
the strength of the research, and the methods and results section are refreshingly thorough.
Main points:
*Abstract - The methods/results sections of the main paper are easy to follow and understandable,
however at times the corresponding sections in the abstract are difficult to follow. Consider
simplifying the abstract.
*It is unclear at times whether the research is located in end of life care for those with chronic
conditions, or specifically for older adults. A sentence stating that the setting is open to adults,
however is predominantly utilised by older adults, would clarify this.
*At times, the introduction and discussion feel slightly abstract in reference to the experience of
patients within these settings. If there is qualitative research available in this area, the paper would
benefit from some discussion of how patients are admitted to such settings, i.e. what differentiates
between those who are discharged to care homes, and the care received.
*The discussion is repetitive of the results at times (pages 11 and 12), this could be shortened and
instead a wider discussion regarding the position and importance of intermediate care units within
the wider long term care system for older adults, and subsequent need for end of life care
provision, could be added.
Minor points:
*Abstract - it is unclear if the study is limited to older adults, or that the setting is
disproportionality used by older adults. It would be useful to clarify this early on.
*Abstract - change 2016 dates to "over a one year period in 2016".
*Abstract - "We explored the cohort by non-cancer and cancer with significant differences in
mortality" - reword this sentence.
*Abstract - "At 0-28 days post-admission, risks were highest (reference: Musculoskeletal
disorders) for respiratory conditions (pneumonia aHR 6·17 [95% CI 4·90-7·76], chronic
obstructive pulmonary disease (aHR 5·01 [95% CI 3·78-6·62]), dementia (aHR 5·07 [95% CI
3·80- 6·77]), liver disease (aHR 9·75 [95% CI 6·50-14·6]) and (reference cancer 'other') lung
cancer (aHR 1·20 [95% CI 1·04-1·39])." - this isn't clear, it may be worth rewording as "At 0-28
days post-admission, risks were highest for XX, XX and XX, when compared to (reference).
Report non cancer and cancer in separate sentences.
*Abstract - "Highest multi-morbidity (reference: lowest) at 0-28 days showed for non-cancer aHR
2·57 [95% CI 2·36-2·79] and cancer aHR 2·59 [95% CI 2·13-3·15]." - reword this sentence.

*Consider changing the aHR to HR and clarify in the text that they are adjusted - the use of HR
would not imply that the hazard ratio is not adjusted and aHR is uncommon in usage (in my
experience).
*Page 7 line 144: "using bidirectional selection with an entry criterion 145 of 0·1 and retention
criterion of 0·05" - clarify that these refer to p values.
*Table 2 - highlight significant findings in bold or star them.
*Figure 1 - second box down needs "cancer admissions" adding.
*Kaplan Meier curves - in my view, the numbers at risk are not required as the figures illustrate the
point well enough.
*The term "unique" is used too often, consider rewording.

Author’s response to reviews:

Dear Dr Lin Lee,
Re: Response to peer review comments on the manuscript‘Characteristics and mortality rates
among patients requiring intermediate care: a national cohort study using linked databases’
Thank you for considering the above manuscript for publication. We have reviewed the peer
review comments received and amended the manuscript accordingly. We thank the peer reviewers
for their consideration of the manuscript and helpful comments. We consider our response has
enhanced the quality, clarity and potential impact of the findings. Overall, the study was viewed as
important for clinical care and policy by conducting robust analysis of national data to address a
relatively neglected area of care for older people. The table below details each reviewers’
comments and our response. All changes made are highlighted in the revised manuscript.
Thank you in anticipation for your consideration of this revised manuscript.
On behalf of the co-authors
Yours sincerely,
Catherine J Evans

Peer review comments and the author response:
Reviewer 1
Thank you for sending me this manuscript to review. It was a pleasure to read. It is extremely well
written and concise in it's reporting. I commend the authors for completing such important work
and adhering to a rigorous methodology. I have only very minor comments for the authors, which I
leave to their discretion as to whether or not any changes are made. As I said, these are extremely
minor points as overall, I thought the paper was extremely interesting and of a very high standard
Thank you for your comments detailing the importance and strength of the manuscript.
On lines 171 - 172, it would be helpful to have the percentages to the n values of total numbers
from cancer and non-cancer. I find it really interesting that only 5% of the total sample were
cancer. I am surprised that this isn't addressed more in the results/discussion - particularly in the
light of cancer having the most predictable disease trajectory.
We have included in the results the respective proportional size for the cancer and non-cancer
groups. We have detailed in the limitations the small proportion of the cancer group (4.8%) in the
cohort, potential under-reporting with inclusion limited to cancer as the main diagnosis on the
index, as opposed to a history of cancer (lines 319-321).
Figure 1 appears to be missing some text - in the second box "368......". I assume this is cancer
admissions? If I was being pedantic, I would expect the exclusion arrows on the figure to point the
other way (towards the exclusion boxes).
Thank you, we have corrected this typo. We agree the exclusion arrows are clearer pointing to
the exclusion boxes. We have amended to show this.
I see a reference to SPACE on the authorship list, but no further information is given on this
group.Thank you for noting this omission.
We have detailed in the acknowledgement that the manuscript is part of a larger study, stating in
full the study acronym SPACE, and the Steering groups members (line 374-376).

Thank you this is a helpful suggestion for the title that reflects more accurately the aim of the
manuscript and reporting. We have amended the title accordingly.

Reviewer's report:
Thank you for the opportunity to review this article, the paper reports on a well conducted analysis
in a relatively neglected setting. End of life care for older adults is an important area, and a
strength of this study is its comprehensiveness in sample size and representation of the patient
population. The addition of the systematic review and contextualisation within the findings adds to
the strength of the research, and the methods and results section are refreshingly thorough.
Main points:
*Abstract - The methods/results sections of the main paper are easy to follow and understandable,
however at times the corresponding sections in the abstract are difficult to follow. Consider
simplifying the abstract.
*It is unclear at times whether the research is located in end of life care for those with chronic
conditions, or specifically for older adults. A sentence stating that the setting is open to adults,
however is predominantly utilised by older adults, would clarify this.
*At times, the introduction and discussion feel slightly abstract in reference to the experience of
patients within these settings. If there is qualitative research available in this area, the paper would
benefit from some discussion of how patients are admitted to such settings, i.e. what differentiates
between those who are discharged to care homes, and the care received.
*The discussion is repetitive of the results at times (pages 11 and 12), this could be shortened and
instead a wider discussion regarding the position and importance of intermediate care units within
the wider long term care system for older adults, and subsequent need for end of life care
provision, could be added.
Minor points:
*Abstract - it is unclear if the study is limited to older adults, or that the setting is
disproportionality used by older adults. It would be useful to clarify this early on.
*Abstract - change 2016 dates to "over a one year period in 2016".
*Abstract - "We explored the cohort by non-cancer and cancer with significant differences in
mortality" - reword this sentence.
*Abstract - "At 0-28 days post-admission, risks were highest (reference: Musculoskeletal
disorders) for respiratory conditions (pneumonia aHR 6·17 [95% CI 4·90-7·76], chronic
obstructive pulmonary disease (aHR 5·01 [95% CI 3·78-6·62]), dementia (aHR 5·07 [95% CI
3·80- 6·77]), liver disease (aHR 9·75 [95% CI 6·50-14·6]) and (reference cancer 'other') lung
cancer (aHR 1·20 [95% CI 1·04-1·39])." - this isn't clear, it may be worth rewording as "At 0-28
days post-admission, risks were highest for XX, XX and XX, when compared to (reference).
Report non cancer and cancer in separate sentences.
*Abstract - "Highest multi-morbidity (reference: lowest) at 0-28 days showed for non-cancer aHR
2·57 [95% CI 2·36-2·79] and cancer aHR 2·59 [95% CI 2·13-3·15]." - reword this sentence.

*Consider changing the aHR to HR and clarify in the text that they are adjusted - the use of HR
would not imply that the hazard ratio is not adjusted and aHR is uncommon in usage (in my
experience).
*Page 7 line 144: "using bidirectional selection with an entry criterion 145 of 0·1 and retention
criterion of 0·05" - clarify that these refer to p values.
*Table 2 - highlight significant findings in bold or star them.
*Figure 1 - second box down needs "cancer admissions" adding.
*Kaplan Meier curves - in my view, the numbers at risk are not required as the figures illustrate the
point well enough.
*The term "unique" is used too often, consider rewording.

Title: Characteristics and mortality rates among patients requiring intermediate care: a national

Reviewer's report:
The paper aims to investigate the factors associated with death within 1 year of admission to an
intermediate care unit, in order to inform priorities for high-quality care for older people. The
paper is novel and adds value and uses a large sample investigating several factors. However, the
paper is hard to read and would benefit from more clarity and more succinct writing throughout.

Based on my review of the human reviewers' comments and external evidence on intermediate care studies, I can identify some potential issues that may have been overlooked:

## Potential Issues Missing from Human Reviewer Comments

### 1. Diabetes as a Confounding Factor

Diabetes prevalence in elderly hospital populations appears to be significantly high, and diabetes status in combination with cancer was not explicitly addressed as a potential confounder. Medical literature indicates that diabetes care varies by comorbidity type, and diabetes patients often experience worse outcomes from hospital interventions due to medication interactions and condition complexity. In the current study, diabetes may have been grouped under non-cancer conditions without adjustment, which could mask its differential impact on mortality across admissions. This is a consequential issue because diabetes independently increases mortality risk in elderly patients and has drug interactions that affect intermediate care interventions.

### 2. Functional Status and Frailty Assessment

Neither the reviewers nor the authors appear to have explicitly questioned the inclusion of functional status or frailty measures in the mortality analysis. Multiple chronic conditions often correlate with functional decline, but functional status is distinct from disease diagnosis. Medical literature consistently shows frailty status as a strong independent predictor of mortality in elderly care settings. If intermediate care units differed in their ability to assess and manage functional decline, and this was not controlled for, mortality associations could be driven by facility capabilities rather than patient diagnoses (cancer vs. non-cancer). This limitation was not identified by the reviewers but would substantially impact the interpretation of mortality differences.

### 3. Socioeconomic Deprivation Variations

The study does not appear to have controlled for area-level socioeconomic deprivation. Published literature on UK HES data studies shows that Townsend deprivation index and similar measures strongly predict health outcomes, including mortality. Intermediate care units vary geographically across England, and deprivation levels correlate with both health status and intermediate care access. Without controlling for this variable, mortality differences between cancer and non-cancer groups might reflect underlying deprivation patterns rather than disease-specific differences. The reviewers noted ethnic representation concerns but did not explicitly raise socioeconomic factors.

### 4. Vaccination Status Impact on Post-Discharge Mortality

Vaccination status (influenza and pneumococcal vaccines) was not examined as a potential covariate. Literature from 2016-2017 seasons shows these vaccines had variable effectiveness in elderly populations and were inconsistently administered. Since the study followed patients for one year, post-discharge mortality outcomes could be influenced significantly by vaccine coverage differences between groups. This temporal factor affecting the mortality period was not identified by reviewers.

### 5. Data Source Limitations on Patient Functionality

The HES database limitations regarding capturing functional status and frailty were not explicitly discussed. Hospital Episode Statistics data captures diseases and diagnoses but does not systematically record functional assessments or frailty scores. This limitation affects the ability to control for this critical predictor in survival analyses. The reviewers raised questions about data uncertainties but did not specifically identify that functional status data may be completely absent from the dataset.

### 6. Disease Severity Modification

Neither reviewers questioned whether disease severity was adequately captured or whether it was used to stratify mortality analyses. Respiratory conditions like pneumonia and COPD have variable severity independent of diagnosis category. If intermediate care patients referred as "pneumonia" had different severity profiles than those with "musculoskeletal disorders," comparing raw mortality figures could conflate disease type with illness acuity. External literature on intermediate care indicates severity assessment is crucial for interpreting outcomes.

### 7. Inter-facility Variation in Care Intensity

The study examined 220 intermediate care units but did not analyze unit-level variation in care practices. Different facilities may prioritize rehabilitation versus palliative approaches. Reviewer 3 noted the palliative care integration concern, but unit-level practice variations affecting mortality were not examined. This could explain why some non-cancer patients had better outcomes than the aggregated mortality figures suggest.

## Summary

The reviewers focused substantially on data reporting quality, clarity, and basic statistical methods. However, they did not identify: (1) diabetes as an important comorbidity confounder, (2) the role of functional/frailty status as an unmeasured predictor, (3) socioeconomic deprivation controls, (4) vaccination status during the mortality follow-up period, (5) explicit discussion of functional data limitations in HES, (6) disease severity stratification importance, or (7) inter-facility care variation analysis. These omissions represent important methodological and interpretation concerns that could affect the validity of drawing conclusions about the differential mortality risk between cancer and non-cancer patients in intermediate care settings.

The study's validity would benefit from addressing these limitations, particularly given the public health implications for intermediate care policy and palliative care integration recommendations.
